findings.claim: “He compressed timelines, invented dialogue, and added dramatic devices like the soothsayer’s warning to heighten tension.” Repeated in the Key Takeaways (“added devices like the soothsayer”) and in the lesson’s Plutarch practice question (“invented the soothsayer’s dramatic warning”).
findings.truth: Shakespeare did not invent the soothsayer. North’s Plutarch (Life of Caesar) already carries the seer who warns Caesar of the Ides of March and the exchange “The Ides of March be come” / “Aye, but not gone”, which Shakespeare dramatises at 1.2 and 3.1. Shakespeare gave the warning far more dramatic weight; he did not add it. A student using this for AO3 would make a false source claim.
findings.evidence: North's Plutarch, Shakespeare's source for Julius Caesar (Life of Caesar, 'Caesars day of his death prognosticated by a Soothsayer') — https://shakespeare-navigators.ewu.edu/plutarch_caesar/index.html ; play text lines 295, 301, 313, 1951 of scripts/_retrofc/_texts/julius-caesar.txt

findings.claim: Q3 mark scheme: “the funeral speeches closely follow the source”.
findings.truth: The opposite, and it contradicts the same lesson’s own Key Fact (“Antony’s funeral speech is Shakespeare’s own rhetorical invention — Plutarch’s account summarises the funeral in only a few lines”). Plutarch reports that Antony spoke and showed the bloody robe; the words of both funeral speeches are Shakespeare’s.
findings.evidence: Lesson 1 content_html Key Fact (narration id n4); Plutarch, Life of Brutus 20 / Life of Antony 14 via North — https://shakespeare-navigators.ewu.edu/plutarch_caesar/index.html

findings.claim: Every lesson carries one question typed “30 marks — Essay” whose own mark scheme ladder runs Top band (11–12 marks) down to Lower band (1–2 marks). The stated marks contradict the mark scheme. This recurs in all seven lessons (L1 q2, L2 q6, L3 q5, L4 q5, L5 q3, L6 q3, L7 q2).
findings.truth: There is no 12-mark question in AQA GCSE English Literature, so the ladder is the wrong element, not the label. The Shakespeare question is 30 marks plus 4 for spelling, punctuation and grammar. The same lessons already carry the correct house 30-mark ladder on their Shakespeare essay (25–30 / 19–24 / 13–18 / 7–12 / 3–6 / 1–2), so the fix rescales the twelve-mark ladder onto it and keeps the band names. The alternative — relabelling the type to “12 marks” — was rejected because no AQA English Literature question carries 12 marks.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Specification at a glance (Paper 1, 64 marks, Section A Shakespeare extract plus whole play) and 4.3 (Paper 1 maximum raw mark 64 = 30 + 4 SPaG + 30)

findings.claim: Brutus “even imagines future audiences re-enacting the scene: ‘How many ages hence / Shall this our lofty scene be acted over / In states unborn and accents yet unknown!’”, followed by “Brutus is describing exactly what is happening in the Globe Theatre”. The metatheatre definition and the glossary repeat it.
findings.truth: Those three lines are Cassius’s, at 3.1, immediately after Brutus’s “Stoop, Romans, stoop”. Brutus’s reply is the different speech “How many times shall Caesar bleed in sport”. A student quoting this as Brutus loses credit for attribution.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/julius-caesar.txt lines 2191–2194 (CASSIUS. Stoop then, and wash. How many ages hence / Shall this our lofty scene be acted over / In States unborn, and accents yet unknown!) against BRUTUS at 2184–2189 and 2196–2199

findings.claim: “blank verse” is defined as “A rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.” Same wording in the hover definition inside content_html.
findings.truth: That defines metre. Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter. AO2 credits accurate subject terminology, so a student repeating this definition is wrong on a term this unit tells them to use.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md 4.2 AO2 (‘using relevant subject terminology where appropriate’)

findings.claim: “Cassius asks: ‘If we do meet again, why, we shall smile; / If not, why then, this parting was well made.’ Brutus echoes the sentiment.”
findings.truth: The speakers are inverted. Brutus speaks those lines at 5.1; Cassius answers with the variant “If we do meet again, we’ll smile indeed; / If not, ’tis true this parting was well made.”

findings.claim: Q1 mark scheme rewards “Cassius’s ironic ‘honourable men’ speech turning honour into a weapon”.
findings.truth: The ironic repetition of ‘honourable men’ is Antony’s funeral speech at 3.2. Cassius never uses it. The lesson’s own content and lesson 3 both attribute it to Antony.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/julius-caesar.txt lines 2619 onward (Antony, 3.2); line 2730 (FIRST CITIZEN. They were traitors. Honourable men!)

findings.claim: Q2: “Read Act 4, Scene 3 from the appearance of Caesar’s ghost to Brutus’s line ‘I think it is the weakness of mine eyes.’”
findings.truth: That line is spoken as the ghost enters, before the ghost speaks, so the stated range runs backwards and encloses a single line. The range is reversed so the extract runs from that line to the ghost’s ‘Thou shalt see me at Philippi’, which is what the mark scheme asks students to analyse.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/julius-caesar.txt lines 3852–3870 (Enter the Ghost of Caesar / I think it is the weakness of mine eyes / GHOST. Thy evil spirit, Brutus / To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi)

findings.claim: Octavius “speaks with quiet authority (‘I was born free’ echoes Cassius, but from a position of legitimate power)”.
findings.truth: Octavius never says ‘I was born free’. That line belongs to Cassius at 1.2 (“I was born free as Caesar; so were you”) — the lesson has handed one character’s line to another. Octavius’s quiet-authority lines at Philippi are “I was not born to die on Brutus’ sword” and, overruling Antony, “I do not cross you; but I will do so.” The second is used in the fix because it needs no nested apostrophe.

findings.claim: Q2 asks for Act 1, Scene 2 ‘Let me have men about me that are fat’ to ‘He thinks too much: such men are dangerous’, then its mark scheme credits “The third-person self-reference (‘Caesar should be’)”.
findings.truth: ‘Caesar should be a beast without a heart’ is Act 2, Scene 2 — a different scene from the printed extract. The third-person self-reference in this scene is ‘for always I am Caesar’, fourteen lines further on. The extract end is moved to that line and the mark scheme quotation corrected, so evidence and extract agree.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/julius-caesar.txt line 570 (for always I am Caesar, 1.2) and line 1672 (Caesar should be a beast without a heart, 2.2)

findings.claim: “verse” is defined as “Poetry with a regular rhythmic pattern but no rhyme.” Same wording in the hover definition inside content_html.
findings.truth: That describes blank verse. Verse is writing set out in metrical lines and may rhyme — Shakespeare closes many scenes with rhyming couplets. The definition as written would make a student call a rhyming couplet prose.

findings.claim: “Name four omens Shakespeare uses to foreshadow Caesar’s death.” Answer: “Soothsayer’s warning, Act 1 Scene 3 storm, Calpurnia’s dream, Caesar’s ghost.”
findings.truth: Caesar’s ghost appears at 4.3, after the assassination, and foreshadows Brutus’s defeat at Philippi, not Caesar’s death. The question wording is widened to ‘omens or supernatural signs’ so the answer is true; lesson 7 already asks the same list correctly (‘support a fatalistic reading’).

findings.claim: “... embed context (AO3) throughout, and use precise literary terminology for SPaG (AO4).”
findings.truth: AO4 rewards a range of vocabulary and sentence structures with accurate spelling and punctuation. Subject terminology is credited under AO2. Telling a student that terminology earns the four SPaG marks misdirects the easiest marks on the paper.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md 4.2: AO4 ‘Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation’; AO2 ‘using relevant subject terminology where appropriate’

findings.claim: “patricians: Members of the Roman aristocratic ruling class who held hereditary seats in the Senate and dominated Roman politics.” Same wording in the hover definition and in a flashcard answer.
findings.truth: Patrician rank was hereditary, but Senate seats were not — censors enrolled senators, normally former magistrates, and by the late Republic most senators were plebeian nobles. No GCSE examiner would penalise the lesson’s version, so this is recorded rather than edited; it would take three parallel edits to correct.
findings.evidence: General Roman-history reference; no play-text or spec conflict.

findings.claim: Question-type labels do not always match the question: whole-play questions are typed “8 marks — Extract Analysis” (for example L1 q3 and q5, L5 q4, L7 q3 and q4) and an essay-planning task is typed “4 marks — Quote Analysis” (L7 q6).
findings.truth: These are house practice formats, and each one’s ladder matches its own stated marks, so nothing misleads a student about AQA’s marks. Only the label is loose. Recorded for the unit-wide relabel queue rather than edited here. No label anywhere in this unit says ‘Modern Text’ or ‘19th-century’.
findings.evidence: Raw practice_questions type fields across L01–L07

summary: Thirteen fixable findings and two notes across seven lessons, from 26 edits. Six HIGH findings are misattributed or fabricated quotations and source claims: 'How many ages hence' given to Brutus instead of Cassius (L3), the Philippi farewell speakers inverted (L4), Antony's 'honourable men' speech credited to Cassius in a mark scheme (L4), Cassius's 'I was born free' put in Octavius's mouth (L5), and two Plutarch claims in L1 that reverse the truth about the soothsayer and the funeral speeches. Every quotation in the unit was checked against Gutenberg #1522 and all others are verbatim and correctly attributed. Lesson 2 is clean apart from the unit-wide F3 ladder defect, which affects all seven lessons: the question labelled '30 marks - Essay' carries a mark scheme that tops out at 12.
